title: “Secure and controllable”: How Beijing is writing Europe out of its systems – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: An OSW study of 1,600+ Chinese wind-sector procurement documents finds nearly 300 calling for replacement of foreign (including European) equipment as part of a decade-long localisation drive; ECFR's Oertel argues the EU should decide high-risk suppliers at EU level and redefine reciprocity as matching China's protective measures.

insights.claim: A Chinese state-owned utility's June 2025 tender sought to replace controllers for 67 wind turbines at the Kangbao wind farm in Hebei solely because they were imported from Europe, citing risk of being 'controlled by foreign forces'.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Illustrates that functioning European equipment is being ripped out of Chinese energy assets on origin alone.
insights.locator: In June 2025, a Chinese state-owned utility put out a tender

insights.claim: An OSW analysis of more than 1,600 public procurement documents in China's wind sector found nearly 300 calling for foreign equipment to be replaced, with European manufacturers and component suppliers named as risks to remove.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: European industrial-control and wind-component exporters face systematic loss of the Chinese market.
insights.locator: A new study by the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW)

insights.claim: Beijing's substitution of foreign technology follows a decade-plus coordinated three-stage process: creating alternatives, ensuring demand through mandated 'secure and trustworthy' procurement and whitelists, and then replacing foreign vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: The playbook (supply, guaranteed demand, substitution) can be applied to anticipate which other sectors China will localise next.
insights.locator: China’s path to technological self-reliance and control

insights.claim: The 15th Five-Year Plan extends self-reliance targets to industrial-control software, precision bearings, motors, control systems and energy equipment, all areas where European companies retain important capabilities.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: European firms in industrial automation and energy equipment face rising Chinese revenue risk.

insights.claim: Since 2022 major Chinese state-owned utilities have written localisation into their own procurement requirements, objecting to imported systems on practical grounds (reliability, spare-part delivery) and political ones (not 'secure and controllable').
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Policy is flowing down into tender documents, so procurement notices are a leading indicator of exclusion.

insights.claim: China's wind-sector campaign targets software, databases and connected elements used to operate and control power assets, reflecting fear of remote disruption and loss of control over power generation.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Remote-access software in power assets is the dependency Beijing considers most dangerous, and a mirror-image risk for Europe's Chinese-supplied equipment.
insights.locator: In the wind sector, the campaign focuses on systems

themes.theme: EU response: use China's risk map and EU-level designation

insights.claim: The EU should treat China's localisation priorities as a guide to which dependencies Beijing deems most dangerous, and ask whether Europe has an equivalent exposure through Chinese suppliers with remote access.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Chinese localisation targets map onto European attack-surface risks in energy technology.
insights.locator: The EU should treat China’s localisation agenda as a guide

insights.claim: High-risk supplier designations and mitigation measures should be set at EU level because ICT and grid risks cross borders, as the 2025 Iberian blackout showed, and to stop a supplier banned in one member state from shifting business to another.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Expect pressure for harmonised EU supplier bans that could hit Chinese inverter, wind and grid-equipment vendors in Europe.
insights.locator: Designating high-risk suppliers and third countries

insights.claim: Five years after the 5G Toolbox was adopted only 13 of 27 EU states had restricted high-risk suppliers though 22 had the legal powers, and about 60% of Germany's radio access network is still Chinese-supplied.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Shows voluntary EU frameworks fail in practice, making legally binding energy-infrastructure rules more probable.
insights.locator: Five years after its adoption, only 13 of the EU’s 27 member states

insights.claim: The share of European vendors in China's critical advanced communication systems has fallen to less than 3%.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Quantifies the asymmetry that already exists in telecoms, a preview for energy.
insights.locator: The share of European vendors present in China’s critical advanced communication systems

insights.claim: Reciprocity should shift from asking China to open its market to matching China's protective measures, since Beijing's procurement notices name European firms as supply-chain risks while it criticises the EU's revised Cybersecurity Act.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Signals a tougher EU stance on Chinese market access in public procurement and critical infrastructure.
insights.locator: Beijing’s complaints about Europe’s risk mitigation actions

insights.claim: Under the revised Cybersecurity Act the EU should consider whether a third country excludes EU-origin products from critical infrastructure, and use the International Procurement Instrument to address asymmetric procurement conditions.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Watch for use of the IPI against Chinese bidders in EU public contracts.
insights.locator: Under the revised Cybersecurity Act, whether a third country itself excludes

insights.claim: In an increasingly fragmented world with concentrated supply chains, openness is becoming a vulnerability rather than a virtue.
insights.speaker: Janka Oertel
insights.so_what: Supports a durable regime shift toward security-weighted trade and procurement policy in Europe.
insights.locator: Openness itself is no longer a virtue, but increasingly a vulnerability.
